title: Starting the workday
hookLine: a breath and an intention before work

lines: AN EMPEROR WHO WON'T GET UP.
cards: A Roman emperor, writing notes to himself, admits he doesn't want to get out of bed. That's how the fifth book of Marcus Aurelius's Meditations begins: in the morning, when you rise unwillingly.

Today the scene sounds familiar. The laptop opens, the inbox loads, and the first stretch of the day is gone before a single choice has been made. Several traditions put something small at that doorway.

teach.b: First, Marcus. His answer to himself is blunt: remember that you are rising to do the work of a human being. Why grumble about doing the very thing you exist for?
Were you made to lie under the blankets and keep warm? Then he points outside: the little plants, the birds, the ants, the spiders, the bees, each working at its part of the world. Second, a psalm.

teach.h: ESTABLISH THE WORK OF OUR HANDS.
teach.b: Psalm 90 carries the heading a prayer of Moses, and its last verse, in the King James Bible, is a request about work: "and establish thou the work of our hands upon us; yea, the work of our hands establish thou it."
The request comes twice in one verse. If you pray, it's a line ready-made for the start of a workday. Third, a doorway from Islam.

A hadith in the collection of Abu Dawud tells of words the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, taught for leaving the house: in the name of God, I put my trust in God, there is no might and no power except with God.
Bismillah, in the name of God, is a phrase Muslim practice sets at the start of ordinary things: a meal, a journey, a task. Fourth, the breath.
The Vietnamese teacher Thich Nhat Hanh taught people to stop and breathe before ordinary acts, even before picking up a ringing phone. Put together, they make a very small practice.
Not a ritual to adopt, just a doorway between the rest of life and the job: one breath, then one sentence.
What is this work for, today? Then open the inbox.

how: Muslims begin ordinary acts with bismillah, in the name of God; some Jews and Christians pray Psalm 90:17 over their work; readers of Marcus Aurelius return to Meditations 5.1 on hard mornings.

games.q: you're Marcus Aurelius, warm under the blankets on a hard morning. what does he tell himself?
o: stay a little longer; rest is earned.
I am rising to the work of a human being.
an emperor doesn't need to rise early.
games.why: he reminds himself he rises to do a human being's work, and points to the plants, the birds, the ants and the bees, each doing its part.

practice: Picture the place where your work begins, a desk, a counter, a car, a classroom, and before anything opens, take one full breath, slower than usual, and let it out all the way.

Name the work ahead in a few words, then one intention for it: careful, kind, patient, brave, whatever fits. If you pray, you can use a line your tradition already has, like the psalm's or the bismillah, and then simply breathe.

wordCard.voice: Marcus Aurelius. The Roman emperor who told himself, rising unwillingly, that he was made for the work of a human being. Today's word.
